title: ‘It’s shocking really’: Devon community tracks River Dart sewage spills
summary:
Citizen environmentalists create online platform that flags spills in real time and highlights repeatedly polluted spots

The easy thing for the people who live on the banks of the River Dart in Devon might have been to grumble and groan about the sewage spills that blight their beloved waterway.

Instead, citizen environmentalists in the area have created a unique online platform that flags up spills in real time, highlights spots that are repeatedly polluted, and sets out where improvement work is planned – and where it isn’t.

Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian Our rivers Water ‘It’s shocking really’: Devon community tracks River Dart sewage spills Citizen environmentalists create online platform that flags spills in real time and highlights repeatedly polluted spots Steven Morris Sat 3 Oct 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 04.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The easy thing for the people who live on the banks of the River Dart in Devon might have been to grumble and groan about the sewage spills that blight their beloved waterway. Instead, citizen environmentalists in the area have created a unique online platform that flags up spills in real time, highlights spots that are repeatedly polluted, and sets out where improvement work is planned – and where it isn’t. Friends of the Dart (FOD) , an independent, not-for-profit organisation, says its River Hub is the first platform to pull together, overflow by overflow, such a sweep of granular detail about how one British river is being polluted. It argues it should be up to water companies or the Environment Agency to provide this sort of information in a user-friendly way – but claims they don’t – so it has done the digging and provided what it believes is a vital service. View image in fullscreen Rob Worthington, one of the designers of the River Hub platform, said it was built to ‘help channel’ anger over sewage pollution. Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian Rob Worthington, one of the designers of the platform, said there was a lot of justified anger about sewage. “We built River Hub to help channel that constructively: to show where the problems are and why, so communities can help decide what gets fixed first.” The launch comes in the week that South West Water (SWW) was fined almost £8m for sewage spills, including in Cornwall’s River Camel, which like the Dart rises on the moors and plunges down to cherished tourist hotspots. It also coincides with the prime minister, Andy Burnham, telling the Labour conference that water was a symbol of what had gone wrong with Britain and promising to reverse Margaret Thatcher’s “ideological ban” on the public ownership of water companies. Worthington told the Guardian about River Hub while sitting on a bench at Steamer Quay on the Dart in the market town of Totnes. This is a designated bathing water spot – but Worthington says he would not swim there, knowing about what goes on a little farther upstream. View image in fullscreen The Kilbury wastewater treatment works, near Buckfastleigh, upstream of Totnes. Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian The hub has a page that people can check to find out where spills are happening right now and where they stopped in the last 12 hours. There is also information about “dry spills” – discharges when there was no or little rain. Worthington acknowledged other independent sewage maps, such as Top of the Poops , also do this job. “But River Hub takes this a lot further,” he said. A section called Why it keeps happening? probes issues such as whether sewage treatment works have the capacity to deal with the sewage produced by the size of the population it serves. The hub concludes that not all do. In Who is fixing it?, the hub spells out works that are taking place or planned, with the dates they are due to be completed, and also draws attention to problem spots where there is no planned remedial work. A lengthy How we know? section sets out the hub’s methodology – for example, where the rainfall data it uses to classify each dry spill comes from. View image in fullscreen People who live in and around Totnes tell tales of falling ill after swimming in the Dart and its tributaries. Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian Much of the data used, such as SWW spill information and permits, is in the public domain but some of it can be difficult to spot, and FOD had to extract some through freedom of information requests. Worthington has worked on the hub alongside his day job as a business analyst and accepted that the picture the platform provided was incomplete and there could be inaccuracies.
